vignette:
Robert was fifty-six, a pianist who had spent thirty years in recording studios and small venues, known for his steady hands and his ability to read a room. That steadiness ended two years ago, one night after a session, when a colleague he trusted followed him to his car. The man wore a heavy cologne-something woody, sweet-and when Robert refused his advances, the violence came fast: a blow to the face that split his lip, then a hand clamped over his mouth, blood smearing across his own cheek, the scent of the cologne flooding his nose as the assault unfolded. He remembered that smell with unbearable clarity. He remembered the blood on his tongue. But other parts-how he got home, what he said to his wife, the hours that followed-were blank, as if someone had erased them. He could not tell a coherent story of what happened, even to himself.

In the months afterward, Robert found that whenever a memory fragment began to surface-the weight of a hand, the metallic taste-he would mentally shove it away before it could fully take shape. But even after he pushed it down, the memory had already done its work: for hours afterward, any sudden sound or hint of cologne felt like an incoming threat, and the smallest trigger-a door closing too hard, a stranger stepping close-sent his pulse racing as if the assault were beginning again. That pushing had become automatic: a way to survive. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger about what had been done to him, because anger felt like a door to something he could not control. And he began avoiding people in authority-police officers, uniformed security guards-because they made him feel small and powerless all over again. He also stopped seeing the friends he had socialised with before the assault; their faces belonged to a time he could no longer inhabit, and their casual questions about his quietness felt like accusations.

The world outside his home grew dangerous. Robert only felt safe in a very limited number of places: his studio, the room where he practiced, the corner of the couch where he could see both doors. Any sudden movement by his wife or a passerby put him immediately on guard. And when he was in that state of high alert, scanning for danger, the memory of that night would often rise up unbidden-the weight of the hand, the smell of the cologne-as if the threat itself had summoned the image to confirm that his fear was justified. His irritability spiked; he snapped at his wife for walking up behind him, for touching his shoulder without warning. When he caught a whiff of a sweet, woody cologne in a grocery store, his entire body locked into high alert-a racing pulse, a clammy chill-and he left the cart abandoned. The same happened when he saw blood, even a paper cut, or violence on a screen. His hypervigilance made him scan every scent, every gesture, every hint of force; the more he scanned, the more triggers he found. And the very act of trying to recall the assault caused him to become acutely aware of potential threats around him, as if the memory sharpened his danger radar.

A cycle had tightened over the months. A sudden movement from his wife triggered a flash of the assault-the hand, the weight-and that flash left him feeling exposed, which in turn made him more vigilant, more irritable, more likely to notice a cologne or a raised voice. His avoidance of authority figures and old social contacts narrowed his life, but it also primed him: every rare encounter with a former friend or a security guard became a powerful trigger, because his system had been sensitized by isolation. And by deliberately suppressing his anger and dodging anything that might remind him of that night, he kept his memory fragmented; the story never cohered, the blank spaces never filled, and the partial clarity of the bloody moments remained frozen.

Eventually, Robert stopped accepting gigs that required him to enter unfamiliar venues. His income shrank, and his wife began sleeping in the guest room after he woke her one night screaming, unable to say what he had seen. It was she who finally urged him to call a therapist. He came to the first session with his hands clenched on his knees, afraid that if he let the memories finish forming, he would fall apart completely. But he was also afraid of staying where he was-afraid that the safe zone would keep shrinking until there was nothing left of the musician he used to be.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that the memory causes or amplifies triggers; triggers are externally driven and not shown as resulting from the memory.
No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat leads to the memory; instead, triggers lead to memory and memory leads to threat.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph conveys that the memory causes or amplifies triggers; triggers are externally driven and not shown as resulting from the memory.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph conveys that a sense of threat leads to the memory; instead, triggers lead to memory and memory leads to threat.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
